title: Technical Advocacy Playbook — Inference Risk Mitigation and Pilot Positioning
author: Aisha Patel
body:
Summary:

This playbook is designed for technical advocates and sales engineers driving inference pilots with mid-market and enterprise prospects. It combines positioning and messaging focused on production economics, a compact competitive brief, pilot pricing scenarios, a slide-by-slide pitch outline, a short customer case vignette, and a security FAQ tailored to common enterprise concerns. Use this as the canonical single-page resource when preparing demos, presales calls, and proposal attachments.

Audience:
- Sales engineers and technical account managers
- Solutions architects and platform engineering buyers
- GTM reps prepping enterprise pilots

Purpose:
- Reduce time to a signed pilot by providing repeatable messaging and defensible technical answers.
- Surface mitigations for the top five technical/operational risks prospects raise during evaluation.
- Standardize pilot pricing and success criteria to speed approvals.

1) One-line positioning and 3 supporting messages:
- One-line: Redwood Inference unifies high-throughput, low-latency model serving with predictable economics and enterprise controls across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.
- Supporting messages:
  - Production economics: measurable token cost savings via batching, prefix caching, and model recommendation guidance; we instrument cost drivers at token and route level.
  - Reliability and fallbacks: multi-variant routing, region-aware fallback, and canary/A-B rollouts keep customer apps within latency SLOs.
  - Security and compliance: private control plane options, KMS integrations, and audit logs to meet enterprise governance requirements.

2) Top prospect objections and suggested responses (concise):
- Objection: "We can't risk leakage of PII or IP during pilot."
  - Response: Offer private deployment or Dedicated environment; enable end-to-end encryption, tenant-specific KMS, and redact/disable analytics export for pilot traffic.
- Objection: "Latency spikes will break product UX."
  - Response: Propose a latency SLO for pilot (e.g., p95 < 200ms for single-turn prompts), demonstrate routing and autoscale policies, and run a short perf test (5k synthetic requests) before live traffic.
- Objection: "Proprietary model performance vs open models."
  - Response: Provide side-by-side evals on representative prompts, recommend model variant with lower token cost for bulk inference, and outline rollback/auto-fallback to higher-capacity variants.

3) Compact competitive brief (table represented in bullets to keep doc-friendly):
- Competitor: Large AI Cloud Provider (managed endpoints)
  - Strengths: broad model catalog, integrated cloud infra, enterprise trust brand.
  - Weaknesses: opaque per-model performance, coarse-grained autoscaling semantics, higher unit cost at low utilization.
  - Redwood counter: transparent per-token analytics, developer SDKs + runtime knobs (batching, cache), predictable pricing for reserved capacity.
- Competitor: In-house self-hosted runtime
  - Strengths: complete control, data never leaves network.
  - Weaknesses: heavy ops burden, variable performance, engineering time to reach production SLOs.
  - Redwood counter: private deployment option (customer-managed VPC) + onboarding automation and runbooks to reduce time-to-prod.
- Competitor: Other inference platform vendors
  - Strengths: niche optimizations or model partnerships.
  - Weaknesses: fragmented tooling, fewer observability primitives, limited rollout mechanisms.
  - Redwood counter: unified runtime + rollout policies (canary/A-B/fallback) and token-level cost tracing.

4) Pilot pricing guidance (three standard scenarios — use these as proposal templates):
- Discovery Pilot (4 weeks):
  - Scope: 50k tokens/day peak, up to 2 model variants, single-region hosted or dedicated trial.
  - Price: $6,000 flat (includes onboarding, 8 hours SE support, perf verification).
  - Success metrics: latency p95 < 300ms, end-to-end error rate < 0.5%, cost per successful interaction within 20% of target.
- Proof-of-Value Pilot (8–12 weeks):
  - Scope: 250k tokens/day peak, model A/B, integration with customer telemetry, basic private network option.
  - Price: $24,000 (discounted reserved capacity + 24 hours engineering support, runbooks).
  - Success metrics: sustained throughput, 10–20% reduction in per-interaction cost vs baseline, acceptable quality (human eval on 250 prompt pairs).
- Short-term Dedicated Ramp (3 months):
  - Scope: client-dedicated GPU pool, full metrics retention for 90 days, SLA baseline (99.5%).
  - Price: Custom quote — typical starting point $45k/month for modest capacity (includes capacity reservation and dedicated support).
  - Success metrics: SLA attainment, predictable unit economics, ops readiness for production cutover.

Notes on pricing: adjust token assumptions for very long context lengths. Always include a 10% buffer for prefix/KV cache warm-up when estimating pilot costs. For prospects prioritizing compliance, factor private control plane onboarding effort into time and cost.

5) Pitch deck outline (15 slides — slide bullets for SEs to copy into deck):
- Slide 1: Title and contact (logo, SE name, quick value statement)
- Slide 2: Why inference economics matter (latency & cost equations)
- Slide 3: Customer pain — real examples (e.g., search latency, chat drop-off)
- Slide 4: Redwood value props (unified runtime, predictable pricing, private deployments)
- Slide 5: Architecture snapshot (hosted / dedicated / private options)
- Slide 6: Observability and cost transparency (token-level charts)
- Slide 7: Reliability controls (routing, fallbacks, SLA)
- Slide 8: Security & compliance summary (audit, KMS, VPC)
- Slide 9: Pilot proposal (scope, price, timeline)
- Slide 10: Success criteria & metrics
- Slide 11: Case vignette (short customer story with metrics)
- Slide 12: Integration checklist (SDKs, client-side libs, telemetry hooks)
- Slide 13: Rollout plan (canary -> ramp -> cutover)
- Slide 14: Appendix: model recommendations and quantization options
- Slide 15: Next steps and decision points

6) Sample case vignette (1-paragraph customer story):
- Customer: EdgeCommerce (mid-market retail SaaS)
- Problem: High per-query cost and inconsistent latency for product recommendations during promotional spikes.
- Pilot approach: 8-week PoV on Dedicated capacity, focused on workload-aware batching and KV cache of session prefixes; human evals on recommendation relevance vs baseline model.
- Outcome: p95 latency reduced from 420ms to 180ms, per-transaction inference cost reduced 27%, and production rollout approved after demonstrating zero-severity incidents during a simulated flash sale.

7) Security FAQ for prospects (top questions, short enterprise-ready answers):
- Q: Where does data go?
  - A: For Hosted customers, request payloads transit our control plane and are processed on Redwood-managed serving nodes; telemetry aggregated for billing is anonymized by default. For Dedicated/Private, customers can choose a VPC or on-prem deployment so data never leaves their network.
- Q: Can we use our KMS?
  - A: Yes — we integrate with major KMS providers (AWS KMS, Google KMS, Azure Key Vault) and support HSM-backed keys for encryption-at-rest in private deployments.
- Q: How is PII protected during model training/inference?
  - A: Redwood does not train models on customer inference traffic. For extra protection, enable PII redaction hooks and disable analytics exports during pilot.
- Q: What compliance certifications do you have?
  - A: Redwood maintains SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 for our control plane; we publish whitepapers for data residency and can provide customer-specific attestations as part of the enterprise onboarding package.
- Q: How do you handle vulnerability management and pen testing?
  - A: Quarterly pen tests are conducted; critical findings follow a 30-day remediation SLA. We share summary reports under NDA and coordinate PRD-style remediation timelines for private deployments.
- Q: Can we run the inference runtime air-gapped?
  - A: Yes — our on-prem package supports air-gapped installation. We provide an installation bundle, deterministic runtime images, and a documented update/rollback procedure.
- Q: How is observability secured?
  - A: Logs and traces can be routed to customer-owned storage or redacted before storage in Redwood's analytics. RBAC controls restrict access to token-level cost data.

8) Pre-flight checklist (what to collect from prospect before pilot kick-off):
1. Representative prompt set (50–200 prompts) and expected concurrency profile.
2. SLO targets (latency p50/p95, error budget, throughput).
3. Data residency requirements and KMS preference.
4. Integration points (SDKs, telemetry endpoint, auth mechanism).
5. Success criteria and sign-off process (who approves pilot success).

9) Pilot runbook (high-level steps and owners):
- Phase 0 — Proposal: SE creates scope, pilot price, and slide deck. Owner: SE.
- Phase 1 — Onboarding (week 0–1): account provisioning, KMS + networking setup, upload prompt set. Owner: Solutions Engineering.
- Phase 2 — Baseline measurement (week 1): synthetic perf tests + quality evals. Owner: SE + Customer Eng.
- Phase 3 — Traffic test (week 2–3): shadow traffic and incremental ramp. Owner: Customer Platform + Devrel.
- Phase 4 — Evaluation & sign-off (week 4–8): deliver report with cost/latency/quality results and recommend next steps (dedicated, private, or scale hosted). Owner: SE + Customer Success.

10) Appendix: example curl snippet to submit an inference request (copyable):
- curl -X POST https://api.redwood-inference.example/v1/generate \n  -H "Authorization: Bearer <TOKEN>" \n  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \n  -d '{"model":"rwd-llm-1", "input":"Summarize the following customer complaint...", "max_tokens":256}'

Conclusion and next steps:
- Use this playbook to standardize pre-sales responses and to accelerate pilot approvals.
- Before customer calls, adapt the pilot scope numbers to the prospect's concurrency and context length; reuse the Pre-flight checklist as an agenda.
